question: A masthead light is defined under the Inland Navigation Rules as a white light shining continuously over an arc of the horizon of how many degrees?
choice_b: 112.5 degrees, covering only the vessel's forward starboard quarter
choice_c: 225 degrees, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side
choice_d: 60 degrees, covering only the area directly in front of the bow
explanation: The Inland Navigation Rules define a masthead light as a white light placed over the vessel's fore-and-aft centerline showing an unbroken light over an arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.

question: Each sidelight (the red port light or green starboard light) on a vessel must be visible over an arc of the horizon of approximately how many degrees?
choice_a: 360 degrees, the same as an all-round light
choice_b: 225 degrees, the same arc as a masthead light
choice_c: 20 degrees, a very narrow forward-facing beam
choice_d: 112.5 degrees, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on its respective side
explanation: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, each sidelight is designed to show light over an arc of 112.5 degrees on its respective side, from dead ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam, so a red or green light alone tells another boater which side of a vessel they are viewing.

question: A sternlight is defined as a white light shown near the stern of a vessel covering an arc of the horizon of how many degrees?
choice_a: 135 degrees, 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side of the vessel
choice_b: 225 degrees, the same arc as a masthead light
choice_d: 90 degrees, covering only the port quarter
explanation: The sternlight is defined as a white light placed as nearly as practicable at the stern, showing an unbroken light over an arc of 135 degrees, 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side, so an overtaking vessel astern can identify another vessel's position.

question: Under the minimum light-visibility standards in the Inland Navigation Rules, a sidelight on a recreational vessel less than 12 meters long must be visible from at least what distance?
choice_c: A sidelight has no minimum visibility distance
explanation: For vessels of less than 12 meters in length, the Inland Rules set a minimum visibility of 1 nautical mile for sidelights (and 2 nautical miles for the masthead, stern, and all-round lights), so other boats have enough warning distance to react.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.22 (Rule 22) visibility of lights, vessels under 12 meters

question: A sailing vessel or a vessel under oars that is less than 7 meters in length is permitted what alternative to displaying full sidelights and a sternlight, if showing them is not practicable?
choice_a: It may operate completely unlit with no exceptions
choice_b: It must still install full-size sidelights regardless of size
choice_c: It may instead exhibit an all-round white light, or have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light to be shown in time to prevent a collision
choice_d: It may substitute a single red light only
explanation: The Inland Rules give small sailing vessels and vessels under oars (under 7 meters) an exception: if it is not practicable to carry the normal sidelights and sternlight, the vessel may show an all-round white light, or simply keep an electric torch or lighted lantern ready to show a white light in time to avoid a collision.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25 (Rule 25) sailing vessels underway and vessels under oars

question: Which small vessel is exempt from having to display an anchor light or shape at night under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Any vessel under 20 meters anchored anywhere
choice_b: Every anchored vessel, regardless of size or location
choice_c: A vessel over 50 meters anchored in open water
choice_d: A vessel under 7 meters in length anchored somewhere that is NOT in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or other area where vessels normally navigate
explanation: The Inland Rules exempt a vessel of less than 7 meters in length from displaying anchor lights or shapes when it is anchored somewhere that is not in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or other area where vessels normally navigate; outside that narrow exception, anchor lights are required.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.30 (Rule 30) anchored vessels, small vessel exception

question: Besides sidelights and a sternlight, what optional additional lights may a sailing vessel underway exhibit at or near the top of its mast, where they can best be seen?
choice_a: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper light red and the lower light green
choice_d: Two green all-round lights, one above the other
explanation: A sailing vessel underway may, in addition to its sidelights and sternlight, exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the top of the mast, with the upper light red and the lower light green, though this option cannot be combined with the alternative single tri-color masthead lantern.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.25 (Rule 25) sailing vessels underway, optional mast lights

question: Under the Inland Navigation Rules, is a recreational vessel less than 12 meters in length required to carry a whistle or bell on board?
choice_a: Yes, every vessel regardless of size must carry both a whistle and a bell
choice_b: No -- it is not required to carry a whistle or bell, but it must still be provided with some other means of making an efficient sound signal
choice_c: No sound-signaling device of any kind is required on any recreational vessel
choice_d: Yes, but only a bell is required, never a whistle or horn
explanation: Vessels under 12 meters are not required to carry a whistle or bell that meets the technical whistle/bell specifications, but the Inland Rules still require them to have some other means of making an efficient sound signal, such as a canned air horn.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.33 (Rule 33) equipment for sound signals, vessels under 12 meters

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel underway sound if it has stopped and is making no way through the water?
choice_b: No sound signal is required once the engine is stopped
choice_c: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with an interval of about 2 seconds between them, repeated at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_d: Five short, rapid blasts every 30 seconds
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water sounds two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes -- distinguishing it from a power-driven vessel underway and making way, which sounds a single prolonged blast.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35 (Rule 35) sound signals in restricted visibility

question: In restricted visibility, a sailing vessel underway, a vessel not under command, and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver all sound which fog signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes?
choice_b: One short blast followed by one prolonged blast
choice_c: Continuous ringing of a bell only, with no whistle signal
choice_d: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
explanation: In restricted visibility, sailing vessels, vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, vessels engaged in fishing, and vessels towing or pushing sound one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35 (Rule 35) sound signals in restricted visibility

question: What sound signal must a vessel at anchor sound in restricted visibility, such as dense fog?
choice_a: Ring the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute
choice_c: Three short horn blasts every minute
choice_d: No sound signal is required while at anchor
explanation: A vessel at anchor in restricted visibility must ring its bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute, distinct from the whistle-based signals used by vessels underway; vessels 100 meters or more also sound a gong immediately after the bell.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35 (Rule 35) sound signals in restricted visibility, vessel at anchor

question: Under the maneuvering and warning signals in the Inland Navigation Rules, what does three short horn blasts mean?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side
choice_c: I am altering course to starboard
choice_d: I do not understand your intentions
explanation: Three short blasts is the signal meaning 'I am operating astern propulsion,' distinct from one short blast (leaving you on my port side) and two short blasts (leaving you on my starboard side).

question: What sound signal should a power-driven vessel give when leaving a dock or berth, to warn nearby traffic it is getting underway?
choice_a: Five or more short, rapid blasts
choice_d: No signal is required when leaving a dock
explanation: A vessel leaving a dock or berth sounds one prolonged blast to alert nearby vessels that it is getting underway, similar to the signal used when approaching a bend where other traffic may be hidden from view.

question: Under New Jersey law, personal watercraft (PWC) may legally be operated only during which period, which is why PWC operators rarely need to rely on the nighttime navigation-light rules?
choice_b: At any hour of the day or night, as long as navigation lights are displayed
choice_c: Only on weekends, regardless of the time of day
choice_d: Only between sunrise and sunset and during times of good visibility -- PWCs are prohibited from operating after dark or in restricted visibility
explanation: New Jersey law restricts personal watercraft operation to daylight hours in good visibility -- operating a PWC between sunset and sunrise, or in fog or other restricted visibility, is prohibited, which is why the Navigation Rules' nighttime and reduced-visibility lighting requirements come up far less often for PWCs than for other boats.
source_note: New Jersey Office of the Attorney General, personal watercraft law summary (njoag.gov); NJ State Police Marine Services boating equipment requirements (nj.gov/njsp)
